title: Way Seeking Mind
speaker: Seiu Hannah Sullivan
summary: Seiu Hannah Sullivan's talk emphasizes the importance of cultivating a deep sense of connection and purpose through spiritual practice, drawing from their own journey of self-discovery and exploration. They share how their experiences, both challenging and transformative, have helped them develop a deeper understanding of themselves and the world around them, ultimately leading to a greater commitment to their Buddhist practice. Through their story, they invite listeners to reflect on their own path and find meaning in their own spiritual journey.

sentences.text: Shall we do the chant?
Yes, please.
*And unsurpassed penetrating and perfect Dharma is rarely met with even in 100,000 million vows.
Having it to see and hear and listen to, to remember and accept by vow to taste the truth of the Tathagata's words.*
Well, good morning, everyone, and thank you so much for being here.
Everybody, I hope you can hear me.
I'm unmuted.
So let it begin.
We are devoting one precious whole day of our lives to the sangha, and I recognize the choice that you've made to formally practice and to listen.

I join the speakers who ask us to acknowledge and thank the first peoples who inhabited the ground we hover over: the [unclear: "Lami"], the [unclear: "Nukesak"], the Salish people, and the home country of the upper Skagit.
And thank you to the Dharma teachers I've had the honor to study with: [unclear: "Asen"] Goenka, Peter Levitt, Norman Fischer, Tim Burnett, and Kathy Fisher.
And to honor an ancestor: today is my dad's birthday.
He would have been 102.
So before I launch into the story of me, may I point out the irony that the theme of our practice period is a teaching that begins with the directive to drop the focus of self.
I have an early memory.
In it, I'm lying in a bed, imagining step by step the world beyond.
First me, then my family in our house, then our neighborhood in Minneapolis, then the city, the state, the country, the continent, the planet, the solar system, the galaxy, outer space.
And then it gets a little giddy, fluttering in the stomach, a big "I don't know," because it's so huge, so indescribable, so elusive, empty, boundless even.
Sounds like the Zen state was right there, right then.
How ironic that I would devote so much of my life to finding what was already right there.
As I prepared myself for this talk, I thought of my history in Zen with Dokusan, or for speaking at any of the various specialty meetings I've attended.
Primarily, I so don't want to waste anyone's time.
Second, I always assume my query has already been asked, answered, or could be asked better, more poetically.
Please, I prayed, help me not to be superficial, to not sound dumb or stupid.
Save me from making a fool of myself.
I apologize in advance for any gaffes I might make.
And then I remembered one of the best teachings I've ever been given in this Zen journey.
Thank you, Chris Burkhart.
I was apologizing to her for not coming to one of her classes and telling her how bad I felt about it.
And she stopped me and said, "That's just extra.
What is important is to speak from the heart."
And I realize the layers I have built over the decades to cover and protect my heart, broken many times.
I guess that is what brought me to the spiritual life.
My heart was lost, restless.
One of my earliest memories is of standing off to the side of a group, feeling left out, excluded, brokenhearted.
Was it my years as a fat kid?
No dates in high school.
My mother's early, excruciating death from cancer, at a time when people couldn't even bring themselves to say the word.
My father's grief, medicated with a blanket of alcohol.
Was it looking into the faces on TV of the lines of homeless people being fed Thanksgiving dinner at a local mission?
Or just that simple, frequent admonition: "Eat your food.
People in India are starving."
Or the civil rights movement in America.
Or the Vietnam War, trying to imagine why anyone would go to war.
Is that what ignited my recognition of injustice and depression in the world?
Something wasn't right, and I knew it.

I do have a visual memory of walking into our living room at about 13 and seeing the cover photo of that week's Life magazine: an old man, probably one of the tall-turban Sikhs of northern India, sat on a very steep mountainside in meditation.
I was magnetically drawn.
I wanted that.
But first I had to do what was right in front of me: go to church.
Oddly enough, the place where my social justice gene [unclear: "got mind"] was probably at church.
Methodist Church in Minneapolis meant for me a deep teaching in non-separation, that we are members one of another.
And we used to watch this slideshow, and the slideshow was called Members One of Another.
In it, cartoon images of people sitting in bubbles would be floating, and when the bubbles came near one another, they would intersect.
We couldn't get away from one another.
We were all connected.
Add to that the civil rights movement, and I was ready to save the world.
Martin Luther King said, "Until all men are free, I cannot be free."
The Bodhisattva vow.
So I finished college and headed off to the south side of Chicago to immerse myself in the plight of poor Black youth.

When I figured out that a well-meaning little honky girl is unlikely to bring the underserved African American community to enlightenment, I retreated to the East Coast to see what I could do for a community slightly more like me: white, yet open.
I lived and taught in New England in a university town, and among other things, I caught the yoga bug.
I would say that this was pivotal for my understanding of a spiritual practice, and it has stayed with me to this day.
But my heart was still ailing, and I felt that I was not entirely okay as I was.
I had discovered Eastern thought while in college: Siddhartha, Alan Watts.
I left my Protestant life behind, like springing off a diving board.
That, and smoking pot with my counterculture friends, gave me a sense of a little more belonging in the world.
But I still felt in many ways as if I were outside, looking in on it.
After leaving teaching, I spent some years discovering myself in Colorado.
I discovered, as Wendell Berry puts it in [unclear: "the piece of wild things"]:

*When despair for the world grows in me, and I wake in the night at the least sound in fear of what my life and my children's lives may be, I go and lie down where the wood drake rests in his beauty on the water, and the great heron feeds.
I come into [unclear: "the piece of wild things"] who do not tax their lives with forethought of grief.
I come into the presence of still water.
And I feel above me the day-blind stars waiting with their light.
For a time, I rest in the grace of the world, and am free.*
And wandering through the woods and up and down mountain trails, I felt for the first time the immense spaciousness of spiritual calm.
It was a solitary path, though, including those mornings and evenings of staring into a candle on top of an orange crate altar, asking myself, is this it?
Meanwhile, I had moved to Western Washington, started climbing and hiking in the North Cascades and devouring Gary Snyder verses in the high country.
I slipped one of his little books into our backpacks, dreaming that shared dream.
*Mid-August at Sourdough Lookout.
Down valley, a smoke haze.
Three days heat.
After five days rain.
Pitch glows on the fur cones.
Across rocks and meadows, swarms of new flies.
I cannot remember things I once read.
A few friends, but they are in cities.
Drinking cold snow water from a tin cup.
Looking down for miles through high still air.*
And later this one:
*Pine tree tops in the blue night.
Frost haze.
The sky glows with the moon.
Pine tree tops bend snow blue.
Fade into sky.
Frost.
Starlight.
The creek of boots.
Rabbit tracks.
Deer tracks.
What do we know?*
He made creeping into the Zen realm sound simple.
Now, rereading his work, I see him reference the fact that he was reading Huineng, the sixth ancestor.
I probably saw it then, but it meant nothing.
How wonderful that the passing years have made that real to me now.
I found that a healthy dose of activist tree planting suited my wish for outdoor hard work and a lifelong love affair with big trees.
And I would credit one particular walk through a stand of old growth as a primary spiritual experience.
Later, after settling into life in town, a small group of friends and I formed a weekly meditation and yoga group, and I continued working on that broken heart.
Multiple relationships, usually inappropriate, followed, along with an increasingly large amount of alcohol consumption.
Of course, all the time I was also practicing meditation, yoga, and saving the world in the ER.
Now how do you do that?
It wasn't until I noticed that I was having blackouts that it occurred to me that there was a duplicity in my life well lived, and that I couldn't live that way anymore.
I had to let go of some big things.
Finally, I knocked on AA's door.
I found the 12 steps unbelievably comforting.
Moreover, they seemed really compatible with the Buddhist path.
I think the two gems of that time that I took with me were learning to recognize and let go of resentment, and taking responsibility for everything without self-loathing.
All my ancient twisted karma, I now [unclear: "fully about"].
So the broken heart was getting put back together.
And as fate would have it, in walked Jerry, my husband.
I'd like to say that I healed myself, but honestly, it was the love of this beautiful man for me, just as I was, that put the music into that now functioning heart.
Shortly after that, I started teaching yoga, something I hadn't anticipated but found I loved, and my old teacher self awoke.
Meanwhile, my dear friend Judy had moved to Salt Spring Island in Canada and recommended this new Zen guy on the island who was teaching.
"I think you'd really like him," I remember her saying.
I had been thinking for some time that I wanted a teacher and had met a few in the Vipassana community who I liked, but I just hadn't made the leap.
I'd been attending various weekend Buddhist retreats when I went for a week to Samish Island in 2013.
Listening to Norman Fischer's Dharma talks, I realized that my searching was over.
This was it for me.
Two weeks later, I asked Peter Levitt to be my teacher, and for the next many years made countless trips to Salt Spring Island for practice, each one a [unclear: "gym"].
I also realized that ignoring an established place of practice closer to home was a real gap.
I joined the Red Cedar community and began sitting regularly with the [unclear: "Sansanga"].
We all know what happens when you decide to show up.

Pretty soon I was clacking the clappers, striking the Han, finding the sweet spot on the Mukugyo, learning chants, attending sesshin, tossing flower petals at Rohatsu, and finding myself immersing in a second Sangha.
The efforts of Tim Burnett and key Sangha members had grown this little band of Zen students into a lively community of practitioners.
And I have great respect for all of the years of effort and persistence Tim has demonstrated, holding the space for us.
One day, years later, as you know, I had the privilege of sitting facing into the room during Zazen.
The question "Where have all the women gone?" arrived in my head.
And I realized I needed to study with a woman.
I had met Cathy Fisher when she came to our Samish Island sesshin a couple of times, and a friendship developed.
We talked for a couple of years about how we might best live in the Dharma, and she shared with me her ideas about Dharma friends, a non-hierarchical way of being with practice.

She had spent many years living at Tassajara, Green Gulch and City Center with her husband Norman at the center of San Francisco Zen Center life, and had come to a place in practicing and teaching that felt exactly right for me.
I've always had a sort of divided life.
Working nights, then evenings in nursing divided me from having a regular after-school life.
Having a partner who is deeply tied to place 60 miles away from where I lived and worked gave me a life lived in two places.
I picked a teacher I have to either fly to see or must zoom in, when there's already a Dharma center in Bellingham.
It's been a complex dance, finding clarity about not being able to be everywhere at once and choosing where and when and with whom to practice.

From the start of my Zen experience, I felt sheltered under the umbrella of Everyday Zen, be it on Salt Spring, at Loon Lake with Kate and Michael, dropping in for a day here and there at Seattle Soto Zen, and zooming, sometimes with the Everyday Zen group and with Kathy's Dharma friends group.
Presently, I feel an unexpected sense of ease and joy working with the teacher, Kathy, who I love, who loves me, and who is very good at cutting through illusion.
That's a foreshadowing of our practice period study.
I find sangha wherever I go, and I am so touched that people from the different places that I have practiced have joined us here today.
Committing to a deep practice has seen me through the deaths of both Jerry's and my remaining living parents, as well as the demise and death of my alcoholic brother.
One son works with his mental health diagnosis, currently very skillfully.
A daughter lives with her alcoholic husband and is coming into her own practice.
What every parent knows is that our kids are our teachers.
Only by falling down the hole of judgment and expectation have I learned that these states of mind are also just extra.
So in answer to that girl who sat staring at the candle, asking, is this it?
I would say, yeah.
It just takes its own time to speak to you.
In fact, just this is it.
Thank you very much.
*May our intentions equally extend to every being and place with the true merit of Buddha's way.*
*Beings are numberless.
I vow to save them.
Delusions are inexhaustible.
I vow to end them.
Dharma gates are boundless.
I vow to enter them.
Buddha's way is [unclear: "unpassable"].
I vow to become it.*
